title: B-Complex and Alcohol: Which B Vitamins Drinking Depletes
excerpt: Is it safe to take a B-complex when you drink? Which B vitamins alcohol drains and how, whether B vitamins help a hangover, how much is too much, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you take a B-complex with alcohol? Which B vitamins drinking depletes, whether it helps a hangover, safe doses, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, you can take a B-complex if you drink. There is no dangerous interaction between B vitamins and alcohol, and a B-complex the morning after a night out is safe for most people. The more useful question is the other direction: alcohol works against several B vitamins at once. It cuts how much your gut absorbs, how much your liver stores, and how well your cells can use them, and it pushes more out in your urine. Thiamine (B1), folate (B9), and vitamin B6 take the biggest hit, with riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), and B12 also affected in people who drink heavily. For a social drinker who eats a normal diet, an occasional night out is very unlikely to leave you deficient. A B-complex is a cheap, reasonable way to cover the gaps if you drink regularly. But there is no good evidence that a B-complex prevents or cures a hangover.

**The quick rules:** Taking a B-complex with or after drinking is fine; take it with food so it doesn't upset your stomach. Pick a product near 100% of the daily value rather than a "mega" dose, and watch vitamin B6 in particular, because long-term high doses can damage nerves. If you drink heavily most days, eat very little, or notice numbness, tingling, confusion, or trouble walking, talk to a doctor. Those situations call for testing and sometimes prescription doses, not an over-the-counter pill.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor if** you drink heavily on most days, have numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet, feel unusually tired or short of breath (possible anemia), have a sore red tongue or cracks at the corners of your mouth, take prescription medication, are pregnant or trying to become pregnant, or have liver or kidney disease. **Get emergency care right away** if someone who drinks heavily becomes suddenly confused, unsteady on their feet, or develops double vision or strange eye movements. That combination can signal a thiamine emergency called Wernicke encephalopathy, which needs hospital treatment.

## What Is a B-Complex, Exactly?

A B-complex is a single supplement that contains the eight B vitamins together. They're grouped because they do related jobs: they help your body turn food into usable energy, build red blood cells, and keep nerves and the brain working. They're also all water-soluble, which means your body doesn't hold large stores of most of them (B12 is the main exception) and needs a steady supply from food.

| Vitamin | Common name | Main jobs | How alcohol affects it |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | Thiamine | Turning carbs into energy; nerve and brain function | Strongly affected: less absorbed, less stored, less activated |
| B2 | Riboflavin | Energy production; helps activate B6 and folate | Lower intake and absorption in heavy drinkers |
| B3 | Niacin | Energy production; used directly in breaking down alcohol | Used up processing alcohol; deficiency seen with heavy drinking |
| B5 | Pantothenic acid | Building coenzyme A for energy and fat metabolism | Deficiency is rare |
| B6 | Pyridoxine | Protein metabolism, brain chemicals, red blood cells | Broken down faster by alcohol's by-products |
| B7 | Biotin | Fat and sugar metabolism | Some evidence of lower levels in heavy drinkers |
| B9 | Folate (folic acid in supplements) | Making DNA and red blood cells | Strongly affected: less absorbed, more lost in urine |
| B12 | Cobalamin | Nerves, red blood cells, DNA | Absorption can drop; covered in our [B12 and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol) |

Products vary a lot. Some B-complexes contain close to the daily value of each vitamin. Others pack in 50 or 100 mg of several B vitamins, which can be thousands of percent of the daily value. That difference matters, and we'll come back to it.

## Can You Take a B-Complex and Drink Alcohol?

Yes. There's no known harmful interaction between a standard B-complex and alcohol. Unlike sedatives, painkillers, or some antibiotics, B vitamins don't make alcohol more dangerous, and alcohol doesn't make B vitamins toxic. You don't need to space them out by a certain number of hours.

A few practical points:

- **Take it with food.** B vitamins on an empty stomach can cause mild nausea in some people, and a stomach that's already irritated from drinking is more likely to complain.
- **Your urine may turn bright yellow.** That's riboflavin (B2), which is naturally bright yellow. It's harmless and not a sign of dehydration or liver trouble.
- **High-dose niacin can make you flush.** Some B-complexes use nicotinic acid, a form of niacin that causes warm, red, itchy skin at higher doses. Alcohol also makes many people flush, so the two can stack. If that bothers you, look for a product that uses niacinamide instead, which doesn't cause flushing.
- **Timing is flexible.** Before drinking, with dinner, or the next morning all work. Morning-after is convenient because you're probably eating breakfast anyway, and some people find B vitamins in the evening a little stimulating.

## How Alcohol Drains B Vitamins

Alcohol doesn't just "use up" B vitamins. It attacks the supply chain at almost every step. Here's how, in plain words.

### 1. You eat fewer of them

Alcohol has calories but almost no vitamins. When drinks replace meals, which is common in heavy drinkers, B vitamin intake drops. Even on a single big night, the late-night food that follows rarely makes up for it.

### 2. Your gut absorbs less

Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and small intestine. That interferes with the transport systems that pull thiamine and folate out of food and into the blood. Thiamine absorption is especially sensitive, which is one reason thiamine deficiency is so closely tied to heavy drinking.

### 3. Your liver stores less

The liver is a warehouse for several B vitamins, including folate and B12. When alcohol damages liver cells or causes fat to build up in the liver, that storage capacity shrinks.

### 4. Your cells can't use them as well

Most B vitamins have to be converted into an "active" form before they do anything. Alcohol and its by-products interfere with several of those conversions. For example, acetaldehyde, the toxic chemical your liver makes when it breaks down alcohol, speeds up the breakdown of the active form of vitamin B6. Alcohol also interferes with activating thiamine.

### 5. You lose more in your urine

Alcohol makes your kidneys flush out more water, and some B vitamins, including folate and thiamine, go with it. If you've ever wondered why drinking makes you pee so much, that same effect carries some water-soluble vitamins out the door.

### 6. Breaking down alcohol uses niacin

This one is specific to niacin. The two enzymes that break down alcohol (alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) both depend on a helper molecule called NAD+, which your body makes from niacin. Each drink you process shifts a lot of that NAD+ into its used form. That's not the same as running out of niacin after one night, but it's one reason niacin status matters to people who drink a lot.

## The B Vitamins That Matter Most for Drinkers

Not all eight B vitamins are equally at risk. Here are the ones doctors pay attention to.

### Thiamine (B1): the most important

Thiamine is the B vitamin most tightly linked to alcohol. Your brain and nerves burn a lot of sugar for fuel, and they need thiamine to do it. Severe thiamine deficiency can cause **Wernicke encephalopathy**, a medical emergency marked by confusion, poor balance, and abnormal eye movements. If it isn't treated quickly, it can progress to **Korsakoff syndrome**, a lasting memory disorder. This is why hospitals routinely give thiamine to patients who drink heavily.

Milder deficiency can cause tingling, burning, or numbness in the feet, fatigue, and irritability. Our [thiamine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/thiamine-and-alcohol) covers this in depth, including who needs more than a multivitamin provides.

### Folate (B9): the most common deficiency

Folate deficiency is one of the most common nutritional problems in people who drink heavily. Alcohol reduces folate absorption, lowers storage in the liver, and increases how much is lost in urine. Low folate causes a type of anemia where red blood cells become too large and don't work well, leaving you tired, pale, and short of breath.

Folate matters for another reason: it's essential early in pregnancy for preventing birth defects of the brain and spine. Anyone who could become pregnant is generally advised to get 400 mcg of folic acid daily, and avoiding alcohol in pregnancy is the standard medical advice.

### Vitamin B6: broken down faster

Heavy drinkers often have low levels of the active form of B6. Acetaldehyde pushes it off the proteins that protect it, which leaves it exposed to being broken down. B6 is involved in making brain chemicals such as serotonin and GABA, and in building red blood cells.

### Riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3)

Riboflavin deficiency shows up as cracks at the corners of the mouth, a sore red tongue, and skin irritation. It's mostly seen with poor diets, which often go along with heavy drinking. Riboflavin also helps activate B6 and folate, so being low on it can drag the others down.

Severe niacin deficiency causes **pellagra**, a disease with skin rashes in sun-exposed areas, diarrhea, and confusion. It's rare in developed countries today, but heavy drinking is one of the situations where doctors still see it.

### Vitamin B12

B12 is a bit different. Your liver stores several years' worth, so deficiency develops slowly. Heavy drinking can still interfere with its absorption and how it's handled in the liver. Some people who drink also take medications, such as acid reducers or metformin, that further lower B12. See our [B12 and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol) for details on B12 shots and testing.

## Does a B-Complex Help With a Hangover?

This is the main reason most people search for it, so here's a straight answer: **there is no good evidence that a B-complex prevents or relieves a hangover.** Nobody has run a solid randomized trial showing that taking a standard B-complex before or after drinking reduces hangover symptoms.

The idea is popular because it sounds logical. Alcohol depletes B vitamins, and B vitamins are involved in energy, so topping them up should help you feel less wiped out. The problem is that a hangover isn't mainly caused by a sudden B vitamin shortage. One night of drinking doesn't empty your stores. Hangover symptoms are driven by other things, including acetaldehyde, an immune and inflammatory response, poor sleep, dehydration, and the "rebound" effects in the brain after alcohol wears off.

There are two pieces of research worth knowing about:

- **A small 1970s study on pyritinol.** Pyritinol is a man-made compound built from two vitamin B6 molecules. A small trial from that era reported fewer hangover symptoms when people took large doses before drinking. It was a tiny study, it hasn't been confirmed, and pyritinol isn't the same as the B6 in a normal B-complex.
- **A 2019 Dutch diet survey.** Researchers led by Joris Verster asked people about their food intake and their hangovers. Those who got more niacin and zinc from food reported somewhat less severe hangovers. That's an interesting link, but it was a survey of habits, not a test of supplements, so it can't show that taking niacin pills changes anything.

So where does that leave you? A B-complex is a reasonable thing to take if you drink regularly and want to make sure you're not running low over time. It's not a hangover cure, and it won't do much for the headache, nausea, or fatigue the morning after one big night. For a broader look at what has some evidence and what doesn't, see our guide to [vitamins for hangovers](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover).

### What about B vitamins in IV drips and "hangover" drinks?

Many hangover IV drips and powder sticks include B vitamins. If you feel better after one, the fluids, electrolytes, and sugar are doing most of the work, along with time. The B vitamins are mostly along for the ride. That doesn't make them harmful. It just means you're probably not paying for a B vitamin effect you can feel. If dehydration is your main problem, our [electrolytes and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains what actually helps.

## Who Actually Benefits From a B-Complex?

A B-complex is most likely to be worth it if you:

- **Drink several times a week or more**, especially more than a couple of drinks at a time
- **Skip meals or eat a limited diet**, such as lots of takeout and few vegetables, beans, or whole grains
- **Follow a vegan diet** and don't already take B12 (B12 comes almost entirely from animal foods and fortified products)
- **Are over 50**, when B12 absorption naturally declines
- **Take medications that lower B vitamins**, such as metformin, long-term acid reducers, or certain seizure medicines (ask your pharmacist)
- **Could become pregnant**, since folic acid is recommended anyway (though most people in that situation are advised to take a prenatal vitamin and avoid alcohol)

If you're a light social drinker who eats a varied diet, you probably don't need one. B vitamins are spread widely through food: whole grains, fortified cereals and bread, eggs, dairy, meat, fish, beans, leafy greens, nuts, and seeds. In the US, many grain products are also fortified with thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and folic acid.

### If you drink heavily most days

Be honest with yourself here. If you drink heavily on most days, a B-complex from the drugstore is not enough. The amounts of thiamine in a typical B-complex may be far below what a doctor would recommend for someone at real risk of deficiency, and absorption is reduced in heavy drinkers anyway. See a doctor, who can test your levels and may prescribe higher doses. Also know that stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking can cause withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Shakes, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there are signs to get medical help, not to push through alone.

## How Much Is Safe? Watch the B6

Because B vitamins are water-soluble, people often assume you can't take too much. That's mostly true for some of them, but not all.

| Vitamin | US upper limit for adults (from supplements and fortified food) | What happens with too much |
|---|---|---|
| B6 | 100 mg per day | Long-term high intake can cause nerve damage: numbness, tingling, and trouble with balance |
| Niacin | 35 mg per day (as nicotinic acid) | Flushing, itching, stomach upset; very high doses can strain the liver |
| Folic acid | 1,000 mcg per day | Can hide the signs of B12 deficiency while nerve damage continues |
| Thiamine, riboflavin, B12, B5, biotin | No upper limit set | No clear harm at typical supplement doses |

**B6 deserves the most attention.** Nerve damage from too much B6 is well documented, and some regulators, including Australia's, have issued warnings that it can occur at lower doses than people expect, especially when B6 comes from several products at once. Many "high potency" B-complexes contain 50 to 100 mg of B6 per pill, and B6 also turns up in energy drinks, magnesium blends, and sleep or stress formulas. Add them up. And here's the cruel twist: the symptoms of too much B6 (numbness and tingling in the hands and feet) can look a lot like the nerve damage heavy drinking itself causes. If you develop those symptoms while taking a B supplement, stop it and see a doctor.

**Folic acid and B12 go together.** Large doses of folic acid can correct the anemia caused by B12 deficiency while the nerve damage from low B12 quietly continues. A B-complex that contains both avoids most of that problem, but it's another reason not to stack a high-dose folic acid pill on top of everything else without a reason.

**For most people, a B-complex with roughly 100% to a few hundred percent of the daily value of each vitamin is plenty.** More isn't better once you're no longer deficient. Your body simply excretes the extra of most B vitamins in urine.

## Other Interactions to Know About

B vitamins don't clash with alcohol, but a few clash with medicines or tests:

- **Biotin can throw off lab tests.** High-dose biotin, which is common in hair, skin, and nail products and some B-complexes, can cause falsely high or low results on certain blood tests, including thyroid tests and troponin, a test used to diagnose heart attacks. The FDA has warned about this. Tell your doctor if you take biotin before any blood work.
- **High-dose niacin and cholesterol medicines.** Prescription-strength niacin with statins has been linked to muscle problems. This applies to treatment doses, not the small amount in a normal B-complex, but mention it to your doctor if you're on a statin.
- **B6 and levodopa.** B6 can reduce the effect of levodopa when it's taken without carbidopa. Most modern Parkinson's medicines combine the two, which avoids the problem, but check with your pharmacist.
- **Folic acid and some seizure or cancer medicines.** Folic acid can interact with drugs like phenytoin and methotrexate. If you take either, ask your doctor before starting a supplement.

If you take any prescription medication, a quick check with a pharmacist is the simplest way to rule out problems.

## B-Complex vs B12 vs a Multivitamin

Which one makes sense depends on your situation:

- **B12 alone** makes sense if you have a known B12 problem, eat a vegan diet, are over 50, or take metformin or acid reducers. It doesn't cover thiamine or folate, the two B vitamins alcohol hits hardest.
- **A B-complex** covers all eight B vitamins, including thiamine and folate. It's the most targeted choice if your main concern is what alcohol depletes.
- **A multivitamin** covers B vitamins plus minerals such as zinc and magnesium, which alcohol also lowers. For a regular drinker with an uneven diet, a basic multivitamin may be the more complete option. If magnesium is your focus, see our [magnesium and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol).

None of these is a substitute for food. A meal with whole grains, eggs or meat, and some vegetables before you go out does more for you on the night than any pill.

## A Practical Plan for Social Drinkers

If you want to look after your B vitamins without overthinking it:

1. **Eat before and during drinking.** Food slows alcohol absorption and brings B vitamins with it.
2. **Pick a moderate B-complex or multivitamin** if you drink more than a couple of times a week. Check the B6 amount on the label and count other products that contain it.
3. **Take it with breakfast** the morning after, or with any meal. Timing doesn't matter much.
4. **Hydrate and sleep.** These do more for how you feel the next day than any vitamin.
5. **Drink less, slower.** This is still the only thing that reliably reduces hangovers. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

### Where DHM fits

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and it does a different job from B vitamins: it doesn't replace anything alcohol depletes. Some DHM products, such as [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), already include a B-complex along with milk thistle and electrolytes, so check labels before stacking it with a separate B supplement (and watch that B6 total). If you'd rather keep things simple and add DHM on its own, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a lower-cost, DHM-only option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For a wider look at liver-focused supplements, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## The Bottom Line

- A B-complex is safe to take with or after alcohol. There's no dangerous interaction.
- Alcohol lowers several B vitamins, especially thiamine, folate, and B6, by reducing intake, absorption, storage, and activation and by increasing losses in urine.
- An occasional night out won't make a well-fed person deficient. Regular heavy drinking can.
- There is no good evidence that a B-complex prevents or relieves a hangover.
- Choose a moderate dose, take it with food, and watch your total B6 intake.
- Heavy daily drinking, numbness or tingling, or sudden confusion and unsteadiness need a doctor, not a supplement.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I take a B-complex and drink alcohol?**

Yes. There's no known harmful interaction between a standard B-complex and alcohol, and you don't need to wait a set number of hours between them. Take it with food to avoid stomach upset. If your B-complex uses nicotinic acid, a form of niacin, it may add to the flushing some people get from alcohol.

**Does alcohol deplete B vitamins?**

Yes. Alcohol reduces how much of several B vitamins you eat, absorb, store, and activate, and increases how much you lose in urine. Thiamine (B1), folate (B9), and B6 are affected the most, with riboflavin, niacin, and B12 also lower in many heavy drinkers. An occasional night out is very unlikely to make a well-fed person deficient, but regular heavy drinking can.

**Does a B-complex help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that a B-complex prevents or relieves a hangover. A hangover is driven mainly by acetaldehyde, inflammation, poor sleep, and dehydration rather than a sudden B vitamin shortage. A small 1970s study of pyritinol, a man-made B6 compound, and a 2019 diet survey linking dietary niacin to milder hangovers are interesting but don't show that a B-complex pill works.

**Should I take a B-complex before or after drinking?**

Either is fine, and timing doesn't change much. Many people take it with breakfast the next morning because it's easy to remember and they're eating anyway. Taking it with a meal before you go out also works. What matters more is eating real food, drinking water, and keeping your total intake moderate.

**Which B vitamins does alcohol affect the most?**

Thiamine (B1) is the most important, because severe deficiency can cause a brain emergency called Wernicke encephalopathy. Folate (B9) deficiency is the most common and can cause anemia. Vitamin B6 is broken down faster because of acetaldehyde. Riboflavin, niacin, and B12 can also run low in people who drink heavily and eat poorly.

**Can you take too much B-complex?**

Yes, mainly because of vitamin B6. The US upper limit for adults is 100 mg a day, and long-term high intake can cause nerve damage with numbness and tingling. Niacin above 35 mg a day as nicotinic acid can cause flushing, and folic acid above 1,000 mcg can hide B12 deficiency. Count all your supplements, energy drinks, and fortified products together.

**Is a B-complex or B12 better for drinkers?**

For most drinkers, a B-complex covers more of what alcohol depletes, because it includes thiamine and folate, which alcohol hits hardest. B12 alone makes more sense if you have a known B12 problem, eat a vegan diet, are over 50, or take metformin or acid reducers. A multivitamin adds minerals like magnesium and zinc as well.

**When should a drinker see a doctor about B vitamins?**

See a doctor if you drink heavily most days, eat very little, have numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, feel unusually tired or short of breath, or have a sore red tongue or cracked mouth corners. Get emergency care if someone who drinks heavily becomes suddenly confused, unsteady, or develops double vision or odd eye movements.
